title: The Line
passages:
The Marrow rode the swell like a drunk on a barstool — low, listing, held together by cable ties and prayer. Sol stood at the helm with her bad knee locked and the storm glass clicking in its bracket, each tap a second closer to the season that would eat their mooring whole. Behind her, the tower rose from the gray chop like a tombstone with the name worn off: forty stories of concrete and glass, the top ten still breathing air, the rest drowned in silence.

"Depth line at thirty meters," Wren called from the topside station, fingers dancing over the slate reader. Her voice carried the flat calm of someone who'd watched too many divers forget their own names. "Air mix nominal. Dey, your recorder's green. Don't make me lie to the Factor about why his locker came up empty."

Dey laughed, a sharp bark that didn't reach his eyes. He stood at the gunwale in a pressure suit patched at three shoulders, checking the seal on his rebreather with the easy competence of a man who'd done this a hundred times and planned to do it a hundred more. The indenture brand on his wrist caught the light — a thin white line of scar tissue, seven years bought and paid for, six down and one impossible to go.

"Wouldn't dream of it, Reader," he said. "One big score, right? That's what you told me. One locker, one payout, and I walk off this boat with my name in my own pocket."

"One locker at twenty-eight meters," Sol said without turning. "Not thirty. Not thirty-two. You cross the line, Dey, the money doesn't matter. You won't remember what you paid for it."

"I know the rule, Captain. Thirty meters, memory stays down. Like gravity for the mind." He spat over the side. "My mother told me bedtime stories about the line. So did yours, probably."

Wren snorted. "Your mother didn't have a slate recorder bolted to her chest. Mine neither. That's the difference — we get to see what you lost."

"Then don't look," Dey said. "Let me have the surprise."

He dropped backward off the gunwale with a splash that soaked Sol's boots. The water swallowed him clean — no bubbles, no struggle, just the faint *thrum* of his rebreather fading into the dark. On the reader, his depth counter began to tick: five meters. Ten. Fifteen.

Sol watched the storm glass. The mercury fell another notch.

"Twenty meters," Wren said. "He's coming up on the locker deck. Sol, the Factor's drone pinged us twice already. He wants confirmation on the manifest before storm season locks the harbor."

"Tell him we're working," Sol said. "Tell him the Marrow delivers. Always."

"Even when the cargo's a ghost?"

"Especially then."

At twenty-seven meters, Dey's voice cracked over the comm — steady, professional, describing a sealed locker with a corporate stamp Sol couldn't read from here. *Matsuo-Klein Biologics. Cold-chain intact. This one's worth berths, Captain. Real berths. High ground.*

The counter hit twenty-eight.

Twenty-nine.

"Dey," Wren said. Her fingers froze on the reader. "Depth line. Come up."

Static. Then Dey's voice again, lighter now, edged with something that wasn't humor: *Almost there. Just a little deeper. The lock's jammed — need to work the manual override. Won't take a minute.*

"Dey Okafor," Sol said, her hand closing on the rail until the knuckles whitened. "You cross that line, I'm not diving for you. Not this season. Not ever."

*Copy that, Captain. Just — *

The comm cut. The depth counter kept climbing: thirty. Thirty-one. Thirty-two.

On the reader, Dey's heart rate spiked. His oxygen sat steady. But the slate recorder — the black box bolted to every diver's chest that wrote their hours in code no human could read — began to blink red.

Wren went pale. "He's past the line. He's *past* it, and his slate's still recording."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning whatever he's doing down there, he'll never remember it. And neither will we — unless I rebuild it from the slate when he surfaces." She met Sol's eyes. "If he surfaces."

The storm glass clicked again. Thirty-three meters on the counter, and something in the tower's drowned floors groaned — a sound like a bone breaking under pressure, carried up through water and steel to rattle in the Marrow's hull.

Sol didn't blink. "Winch ready?"

"Always."

"Then we wait. And if he doesn't come up on his own — " She left it there, the threat and the promise tangled together like the cables holding the boat afloat.

On the reader, the depth counter hit thirty-five meters and kept falling.

For a long moment the two of them just watched the counter fall, because watching was all the plan they had. Thirty-six. Thirty-seven. The slate's red eye wrote on.

"Pull him," Sol said finally. "Three tugs on the tether, the winch brings him up whether he likes it or not."

Wren's hand hovered over the tether control, a worn brass toggle that would haul a diver topside faster than any man could swim against. "He's past thirty-five. If I yank him now he comes up too fast, gas in his blood like fizz in a dropped bottle. He'll bend."

"Then yank him slow."

"There's no slow. There's the winch speed or his speed, and his speed is down." She keyed the comm anyway, voice pitched hard enough to cut through water. "Dey Okafor. Tug your tether. Two taps. Let me know you're mine and not the tower's."

For a moment there was nothing but the rebreather — the machine that stripped the carbon dioxide out of each breath and fed the rest back, the reason he wasn't trailing bubbles to the surface. Its rhythm had gone slow and even. Too even. A diver fighting a jammed lock should sound like a man swearing, not a man settling in for the night.

"Air?" Sol asked.

Wren checked the second counter. "He loaded a forty-minute bottom mix. He's used nineteen."

"So he's got twenty."

"He's got twenty he can trust. Below the line the mix does things. He starts breathing like that—" she nodded at the slow, patient rhythm in the comm— "and I don't know if the twenty is real or if he's coasting on the last good decision he made."

Sol looked at the storm glass. The mercury had dropped a full line since Dey went over, faster than the season had any right to fall, and she didn't say so, because saying so made it true. "Keep talking to him. If he answers, he's still up there somewhere."

Wren talked. She talked about the payout, the berths, the seven years he'd bled to buy and the one he had left, the name he wanted back in his own pocket. She talked the way you talk to a sleepwalker on a ledge, warm and steady and pretending you weren't scared. The slate blinked its red eye the whole time, writing down every second he'd never get back.

Thirty-eight.

Then the tower groaned again, deep and long, and a shiver of silt rolled up the comm as a hiss — the sound of a floor somewhere shifting off its moorings, concrete letting go of what it had held for twenty years.

The comm crackled.

"Dey?" Wren's voice jumped an octave. "Dey, key up. Say the lock. Say anything."

His voice came back — but wrong.

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said, bright and easy, exactly the way he'd sounded at twenty-eight meters. "This one's worth berths, Captain. Real berths."

"Copy that," Sol said slowly. "You've got the locker?"

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said. "This one's worth berths. Real berths."

Wren went still. That wasn't a man on a comm. That was a recording of a man, the same eight words in the same bright order, the smile still in them though his mouth was forty meters down in the dark doing something else entirely.

"Dey," she said. "What's the manual override look like? Describe it to me. Right now. New words."

A pause, long enough to hurt.

"Cold-chain intact," Dey said, for the third time, and this time there was a hitch in it, a stutter, like the words were skipping against a groove worn too deep. "Real — real — real berths. Won't take a minute. Just a little deeper."

Sol's hand was on the winch before Wren could stop her.

The winch took up the slack in bites, the brake clacking like a man counting change, and Sol fed it out slower than her hands wanted to.

"He's coming up heavy," Wren said, flat over the gunwale with the boat hook. "Sol, he's *heavy*. That's not one man's worth of heavy."

"Then it's one man and a locker." Sol set the brake. "Talk to me."

"Thirty-one. Twenty-nine. He's not swimming. He's not even kicking, he's just — hanging there like laundry."

The water broke. Dey came up face-down with the rebreather still hissing, one arm over the back of his neck, and lashed to his harness with a lanyard he must have tied himself was a steel case the size of a breadbox, corporate stamp stenciled on the lid, frost furring the seam.

Wren got the hook under his shoulder strap. Sol got both hands in his collar. Between them they rolled him over the rail and onto the deck, and he landed on his side and folded, knees to chest, and made a sound Sol had heard twice before in her life and never wanted to hear again.

"Bends," Wren said. "I *told* you. He came up too fast and the gas came out of solution in his blood, fizz in a dropped bottle, and now it's sitting in his joints like gravel." She was already dragging the deck oxygen over, the old green bottle with the taped gauge, jamming the mask onto his face. "Breathe. In, out, don't fight me, Dey, *breathe.*"

Dey breathed. His eyes were open and wet and entirely present, which was somehow worse.

"Did I get it," he said around the mask.

"You got it." Sol crouched, knee screaming, and put a hand flat on the case. Cold. Properly cold, cold enough to ache. "You got the locker, you got bent, you got an hour of my life back. Lie still."

"Hour." He laughed, and the laugh broke in the middle. "It was twenty minutes. Twenty-eight meters, the stamp, Matsuo-Klein, and the lock was jammed, and I — " He stopped. His face did something small and terrible, the look of a man patting his pockets for keys he was holding. "I had the override. There was a bar you turn. I had it in my hand."

"What color was the bar."

"I don't — " He looked at his own glove like it belonged to a stranger. "Reader. What did I do down there."

Wren didn't answer, because she was reading the mix counter on his rebreather and had gone the color of the sky.

"Say it," Sol said.

"He loaded forty minutes of bottom mix." Wren's voice was very level, the way it got when she was holding something down. "He was under for seventy-nine. The scrubber — the canister that eats the carbon dioxide out of what he breathes back — that's dead. Spent. Fifty minutes, tops, and then he's breathing his own exhaust in a wet loop. He should have come up out of his mind and clawing. He came up *rested*."

"Meaning what."

"Meaning I don't know. Meaning something down there gave him forty minutes he didn't pack." Wren's thumb moved on the reader and the slate's red eye went on writing, patient as a metronome. "Seventy-nine minutes on this slate. Every second of it in code. And I have to sit here and turn it back into a man."

"Then do it fast," Sol said, "because the glass is falling and the Factor's drone is going to want that case sealed and I am not explaining a bent diver to a broker."

They got him into the box — a steel tube off a lifeboat, hand-pumped, the only recompression chamber on the coast that anybody trusted and nobody liked — and Wren swung the door and dogged it, and Dey's face went small and square behind the port.

The deck went quiet. Not calm. Quiet the way a room goes when everybody has heard the same wrong thing and nobody wants to be the one to say it out loud. The case sat in its own little puddle of melt. The storm glass clicked. Somewhere below, the tower let go of another floor.

Dey's voice came through the box, muffled and even and horribly reasonable.

"Seriously. What did I do down there?"

Nobody answered him. Wren looked at the slate in her hands, at the red eye, at seventy-nine minutes of a man's life written in a language only she could read.

Wren sat down on the deck with her back against the recompression box, because the reader wanted a flat surface and her legs had opinions about standing. She jacked the slate in — three brass pins, still warm from Dey's chest — and seventy-nine minutes of code filled the screen.

"Talk to me," Sol said.

"Four things on a slate. Depth, mix, pulse, and the bone track, which is what his skull picked up — his own voice coming back through the water. Above thirty I turn that into an hour in about ten minutes." Wren scrolled. "Below thirty the compression goes stupid and I do it by ear, and the only filler I've got is his own words from before he crossed. So every deep build is part record and part me guessing. That's the job. That's the whole job."

"Charming."

"You want honesty, or you want a diver who can sleep?"

She scrubbed to twenty-eight and let it run. The stamp. The jam. Dey swearing at a bar he had in his glove, bright and cocky and exactly one man. She played that part twice, because it was good, and because Dey was behind a steel door with his knees to his chest and deserved to hear himself be somebody.

Then thirty-one meters, and the sound went flat.

Not silence. Worse. A big room, water moving in it, and Dey's breath slow and patient the way it had been on the comm.

"He found a pocket," Wren said. "Air trapped under a slab. There's a man in it."

Sol crouched, knee cracking like a shot. "There's a *what.*"

The voice on the bone track was old and unhurried and had a laugh buried in it. *Easy, son. You're the first thing with a pulse down here since the spring.* Dey, thin: *Which spring.* A pause long enough to hurt. *One of them.* Then the old man again, practical as a plumber. *Your scrubber's dead. I can hear it in you, that wet tick. Take a pull off mine. Bottle's been sitting here being no use to anybody.*

*Why.*

*Because air's a loan below the line. Breathe off my bottle, you owe me a ride up.*

*Then I'll come back with the winch. Two hours.*

*Sure,* the old man said. *Ivo Salas. Say it back so one of us keeps it.*

*Ivo Salas.*

Then Dey's breath went even, forty minutes of it, easy as sleep, while somewhere in the dark a hand-pump ticked and a case got lashed to a harness and a man said *won't take a minute* in a voice that had already stopped meaning it.

Wren stopped the track.

The deck got very loud — swell on the hull, the winch brake, the pump on the box going *tock, tock* like somebody patient at a door.

"Well," Sol said.

"He took the locker. He didn't come back."

Her thumb found the splice tool without asking her. Eleven times she'd done this. Twelve, now. She marked forty-one ten to forty-seven fifty-two and dragged the ends together, and the gap closed like water. Then she laid his own words from before the crossing over the seam — *just a little deeper, won't take a minute* — and flattened the bone track under them until there was no man in it, no name, no bottle. Just a jammed lock, a dark, and a diver too proud to call for help.

She didn't decide to do it. That was the thing she'd never said out loud. Her hands knew the shape of the mercy and went there.

She played him the build through the port. Twenty-eight meters, the stamp, the bar, the frost on the seam. Up.

Dey listened with his eyes shut. "You made me sound competent."

"I made you sound alive. Take it."

Sol was watching her the way you watch a gauge you don't trust. "What's on it?"

"Lock, dark, you showing off. Nineteen minutes of nothing and a very cold breadbox."

"Nineteen minutes," Sol said, "is a long nothing." She held the look one beat past comfortable, then pushed up off the deck with a grunt and went to see about the lashing.

Wren wiped the reader down. Clean, no copy. Behind the port, Dey's voice came through, easy and reasonable and perfectly awake.

"When's Ivo's turn in the box?"

The pump went *tock.* Wren didn't move.

"Say that again."

"Ivo. Salas." Dey's face swam small and square behind the glass, frowning at her, at the ceiling, at nothing. "You said the order. He's after me, right?"
